INTRODUCTION

1. A new immigration status for frontier workers has been introduced in compliance with the UK’s obligations under the Withdrawal Agreement1. The status has been introduced via the Citizens’ Rights (Frontier Workers) (EU Exit) Regulations 20202 (“The Frontier Workers SI”). These regulations came into force on 4.11.203, except4 Part 2 of the SI (with the exception of regulations 6(1)(b) & 6(2) - see paragraph 2); Part 4; regulation 24 (in so far as it relates to an appeal against a decision made under Part 2 or Part 4), and Regulation 28, which come into force at 11pm on 31.12.20.

1. A new immigration status for frontier workers has been introduced in compliance with the UK’s obligations under the Withdrawal Agreement1. The status has been introduced via the Citizens’ Rights (Frontier Workers) (EU Exit) Regulations 20202 (“The Frontier Workers SI”). These regulations came into force on 4.11.203, except4 Part 2 of the SI (with the exception of regulations 6(1)(b) & 6(2) - see paragraph 2); Part 4; regulation 24 (in so far as it relates to an appeal against a decision made under Part 2 or Part 4), and Regulation 28, which come into force at 11pm on 31.12.20.
1 Withdrawal Agreement, Part 2; 2 The Citizens’ Rights (Frontier Workers) (EU Exit) Regulations 2020 (SI 2020 No. 1213); 3 Reg 1(2)(a); 4 Reg 1(3)
2. This Frontier Workers SI also provides for the restriction of those rights and establishes a scheme for frontier worker permits. These regulations come into force on 1.7.211.
2. This Frontier Workers SI also provides for the restriction of those rights and establishes a scheme for frontier worker permits. These regulations come into force on 1.7.211.
1 The Citizens’ Rights (Frontier Workers) (EU Exit) Regulations 2020, reg 1(2)(b) & 1(4)
Background

3. The purpose of this Frontier Workers SI is to protect the rights of EEA nationals who, as workers1 or self-employed persons2, have pursued an economic activity as a frontier worker in the UK by the end of the transition period on 31.12.20 and wish to continue to do so thereafter (Part 2 of the SI). They have rights under the Withdrawal Agreement, the EEA European Free Trade Association (EFTA) Separation Agreement and the Swiss Citizens’ Rights Agreement (referred to collectively throughout this Memo as “the Agreements”) to continue 
to enter the UK from 11pm on 31.12.20 and work as frontier workers for as long as they continue to be so.

3. The purpose of this Frontier Workers SI is to protect the rights of EEA nationals who, as workers1 or self-employed persons2, have pursued an economic activity as a frontier worker in the UK by the end of the transition period on 31.12.20 and wish to continue to do so thereafter (Part 2 of the SI). They have rights under the Withdrawal Agreement, the EEA European Free Trade Association (EFTA) Separation Agreement and the Swiss Citizens’ Rights Agreement (referred to collectively throughout this Memo as “the Agreements”) to continue 
to enter the UK from 11pm on 31.12.20 and work as frontier workers for as long as they continue to be so.
1 TFEU, Art 45; 2 Art 49

4. Frontier workers’ rights are granted under specified legislation1. Those regulations will continue to apply to all EEA workers covered under the Withdrawal Agreement. This means that frontier workers are entitled to access benefits in the same manner as EEA workers subject to the Citizens Directive 2004/38 currently do.

4. Frontier workers’ rights are granted under specified legislation1. Those regulations will continue to apply to all EEA workers covered under the Withdrawal Agreement. This means that frontier workers are entitled to access benefits in the same manner as EEA workers subject to the Citizens Directive 2004/38 currently do.
1 Regulation (EU) 492/11

5. The Agreements1 require that a frontier worker document scheme is to be implemented by the end of the transition period. In addition, the UK has decided (as a matter of domestic policy) to give effect to the Agreements, for a frontier worker to hold a permit2 which certifies their right to enter the UK as a protected frontier worker from 1.7.21. This Frontier Workers SI establishes a frontier workers’ permit scheme (Part 3 of the SI) under which a protected frontier worker can apply for and be issued with a permit certifying their rights to continue to enter and work in the UK (please see paragraphs 42 - 51 for further guidance on permits).

5. The Agreements1 require that a frontier worker document scheme is to be implemented by the end of the transition period. In addition, the UK has decided (as a matter of domestic policy) to give effect to the Agreements, for a frontier worker to hold a permit2 which certifies their right to enter the UK as a protected frontier worker from 1.7.21. This Frontier Workers SI establishes a frontier workers’ permit scheme (Part 3 of the SI) under which a protected frontier worker can apply for and be issued with a permit certifying their rights to continue to enter and work in the UK (please see paragraphs 42 - 51 for further guidance on permits).

1 Withdrawal Agreement, Art 14; the EEA EFTA Separation Agreement, Art 1; the Swiss Citizens’ Rights  Agreement, Art 13; 2 The Citizens’ Rights (Frontier Workers) (EU Exit) Regulations 2020, reg 6(1)(b)

6. This Frontier Workers SI also sets out the circumstances in which a protected frontier worker’s rights to enter the UK as a frontier worker can be restricted, and a permit can be refused or revoked (Part 4 of the SI), in accordance with the Agreements. It also provides protected frontier workers with statutory rights of appeal, and with a right of administrative review, against certain decisions to restrict their rights (Part 5 of the SI).

6. This Frontier Workers SI also sets out the circumstances in which a protected frontier worker’s rights to enter the UK as a frontier worker can be restricted, and a permit can be refused or revoked (Part 4 of the SI), in accordance with the Agreements. It also provides protected frontier workers with statutory rights of appeal, and with a right of administrative review, against certain decisions to restrict their rights (Part 5 of the SI).

Retained worker or self-employed worker status

16. Under the Withdrawal Agreement1, a worker or self-employed worker can retain their worker status on the same basis as EEA migrant workers are entitled under EU law2. This applies despite the fact that they do not move their residence to the State of work. As long as they worked, or were self-employed in the UK, and meet the conditions for retaining worker status, they can retain their worker status whilst they are either in the UK or in their country of primary residence.

In duly recorded involuntary unemployment - evidence of job seeking 
19. A frontier worker who needs access to benefits whilst they are in duly recorded involuntarily unemployment must register with an employment office soon after they are recorded as duly unemployed. This is in line with established case law1.
In duly recorded involuntary unemployment - evidence of job seeking

19. A frontier worker who needs access to benefits whilst they are in duly recorded involuntarily unemployment must register with an employment office soon after they are recorded as duly unemployed. This is in line with established case law1.

Note: DMs should note that a person who is unable to register with DWP because they are over the financial threshold that qualifies them for access to benefits or because they do not require access to benefits, will still be able to retain worker status. An individual in such a situation will need to demonstrate through evidence that they were job seeking during the period when they were unemployed.
1 Secretary of State for Work and Pensions v MK [2013] UKUT 0163 (AAC)

Compelling evidence of job-seeking

24. When a frontier worker makes a claim for benefits, for example two years after the end of the transition period, a DM will need to look back into the history of the claimant’s status and confirm that they  
 were a frontier worker before the end of the transition period and  
 have maintained that status since the last time their status was confirmed.  
25. This may be difficult in cases where the claimant identifies as a frontier worker who retained their status during a period where they did not make a claim for benefits. In such a case, a frontier worker would not have been subject to any checks by authorities who could confirm that they were job seeking. The person themselves, would therefore need to provide evidence of job seeking during the period they seek to assert that they had retained worker status.  
26. 
The “compelling evidence” test no longer represents a higher threshold than the requirement to prove that a person is continuing to seek genuine and effective employment. Compelling evidence may include
 
 recent job applications in the UK or 
 job acceptance letters of genuine and effective work or 
 a change of circumstance which has significantly improved their prospects of obtaining genuine and effective work or 
 
successful completion of a vocational course which is directly relevant to the field in which they are hoping to work or
 
 awaiting the outcome of job interviews.

Retained status as a result of accident or illness

27. In the same way as any other worker, a frontier worker is allowed to retain their worker status if they become temporarily unable to engage in activities as a worker or self-employed person as the result of an illness or accident1. Leading case law2 on the interpretation of what “temporarily ill” means is equally applicable to frontier workers.

27. In the same way as any other worker, a frontier worker is allowed to retain their worker status if they become temporarily unable to engage in activities as a worker or self-employed person as the result of an illness or accident1. Leading case law2 on the interpretation of what “temporarily ill” means is equally applicable to frontier workers.
1 The Citizens’ Rights (Frontier Workers) (EU Exit) Regulations 2020, reg 4(1)(a) & 4(3)(a);  2 FMB Uganda [2010] UKUT 447 (IAC)

28. A frontier worker will meet the definition of “not primarily resident in the UK” (see paragraph 15 above) for the relevant period if they have been present in the UK for less than a total of 180 days in any relevant 12-month period and they have also returned to their country of residence at least once in every 6-month period, or twice in every 12-month period. 
29. It is unclear for how long or in what circumstances a frontier worker can maintain their status without travelling back to their country of primary residence. Where a frontier worker has not returned to their country of primary residence with the required frequency, they may still meet the definition of “not primarily resident in the UK”, if the evidence provided shows that they had exceptional reasons for preventing them from travelling back to their country of primary residence. 
30. Exceptional reasons for not meeting the travel requirement may include

Retained status as a result of embarking on vocational training

31. There are two circumstances in which a person can retain their worker or self-employed worker status if they have embarked on vocational training. These are  
 when they embark on vocational training after becoming involuntarily unemployed (involuntarily unemployed is defined in the same way as a person who needs to register as a job seeker) or  
 where the person has voluntarily ceased working and embarked on vocational training (in these circumstances, the vocational training has to be related to their previous employment).
